01Why now

Why this course, and why now

An agent is a system component that makes decisions at run time, which changes how you design, test and secure everything around it. This level treats agents as architecture, not as a feature: what they may do, what they must never do, how you know they work, and how you stop them. Its scope is informed by current research and the iSAQB CPSA-A AGENTA module, Architecture for Agentic Software Engineering Contexts; Intellica’s curriculum and credential remain independent.

External reference: iSAQB CPSA-A AGENTA — Architecture for Agentic Software Engineering Contexts. Read 2026-11-27 (curriculum 2026.1-rev5, 31 July 2026): seven sections, 34 learning goals, 15 hours with at least three days of training, 10 technological and 20 methodical credit points within the CPSA-A scheme. Intellica's level is independently designed and does not confer iSAQB credit or accreditation. Only providers accredited by iSAQB can teach the module for credit.

02Outcomes

What you will be able to do

Choose the right shape

Decide when a fixed workflow is better than an agent, and how much autonomy to grant.

Design the boundaries

Define tools, permissions, memory and budgets for an agent system.

Prove it works

Plan evaluations and tracing so you can measure an agent, not just watch it.

Document for agents

Write architecture notes that people and coding agents can both read.

03Syllabus

16 lessons in 4 modules

Module 1Agents as components

What an agent is, architecturally.

  1. Workflows, assistants and agents: choosing the shape
  2. The agentic loop and tools as contracts
  3. Levels of autonomy and the human in the loop
  4. Context and memory as architecture

Module 2Deciding with AI

Use AI to widen your options without handing over the decision.

  1. Decisions as testable hypotheses
  2. Design exploration with AI: options, drivers and review points

Module 3Knowledge and control for coding agents

Make the architecture something an agent can read and cannot quietly break.

  1. Architecture knowledge agents can read: decision records, rules and specifications
  2. Delivering knowledge at the right moment: retrieval, skills and tool servers
  3. A harness of preventive and detective controls
  4. Architecture tests and drift checks in the pipeline
  5. Extracting architecture from existing code, and checking what the agent found

Module 4Running agent systems you can trust

Patterns, limits, evidence and responsibility.

  1. Orchestration patterns and when multi-agent designs help
  2. Failure modes, retries and cost budgets
  3. Evaluation plans and tracing
  4. Governance, law and safe integrations
  5. Keeping judgment: ownership, skill and the architect’s changing role

04The lab

Your agent system design

Design and document an agent system for a real task in your own field, then write the rules and tests that keep an agent inside your design. One project, built in steps after each lesson. Each step has instructions, a finished example, a health check, and saves on your device.

The steps

  1. Describe the task and decide the shape
  2. Define the tools and their contracts
  3. Set permissions, budgets and approval points
  4. Design the memory and context
  5. Turn three decisions into testable hypotheses
  6. Explore design options with AI and review them
  7. Write the machine-readable architecture rules an agent must follow
  8. Design delivery of knowledge and test it
  9. Design the harness: a matrix of controls
  10. Write the tests that prove each rule, or mark it as a human review
  11. Extract an architecture view and verify what the agent found
  12. Choose an orchestration pattern and contain failure between agents
  13. Design failures, retries and cost budgets
  14. Write the evaluation and tracing plan
  15. Write the governance and safe-integration record
  16. Assign ownership and adoption, then write the architecture note an agent could read

What the health check looks for

  • Every tool has a contract, a class and an enforced limit
  • Every rule names the check that verifies it, or a named reviewer
  • There is a stated limit on cost and on actions
  • The evaluation plan names a measurable pass mark

05How you learn

Evidence-led learning method

Worked examples

The professional academies begin with complete examples and make the reasoning behind good decisions visible.

Guided practice

Scaffolds fade as learners progress—from annotated examples to structured tasks and independent work.

Retrieval and review

Low-stakes questions prompt recall; review revisits important concepts. Model answers and rubrics make improvement specific.

Research-informed updates

The academies cite primary research and standards, record review dates and receive versioned updates as evidence changes.

The method follows published research on retrieval practice, worked examples and spaced review. Read the evidence and sources.

A certificate you can verify and share

After meeting the published course-completion criteria, learners can claim a certificate with its own credential ID and a public verification page. The certificate can be shared or saved as a PDF.

To earn it

  1. Finish every lesson
  2. Complete every lab step and pass its health checks

What you get

  • A credential ID and a public page that confirms it
  • Add to LinkedIn in one click

The certificate records completion against the course rules, based on progress reported by the learner’s browser. It is self-reported and unproctored; lab work is not independently marked by Intellica. It is not accredited as a professional qualification and does not confer or replace an external certification.
